rubric.why: Roots hold the plant firmly in the soil.
rubric.description: Gives the anchorage or support function of roots.
rubric.how: Award for stating that roots anchor or support the plant in the soil.

rubric.why: Roots take up water and mineral salts from the soil.
rubric.description: Gives the absorption function of roots.
rubric.how: Award for stating that roots absorb water and minerals from the soil.

modelAnswer: Roots anchor the plant firmly in the soil.
Roots absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.

items.followUp: What causes the first and second heart sounds?

rubric.why: The first heart sound is associated with closure of the atrioventricular valves.
rubric.description: Explains the cause of the lubb sound.
rubric.how: Award for linking lubb to closure of the atrioventricular (bicuspid and tricuspid) valves.

rubric.why: The second heart sound is associated with closure of the semilunar valves.
rubric.description: Explains the cause of the dubb sound.
rubric.how: Award for linking dubb to closure of the semilunar valves.

modelAnswer: The sound lubb is produced when the atrioventricular valves close as the ventricles begin to contract.
The sound dubb is produced when the semilunar valves close as the ventricles begin to relax.

items.followUp: Describe the tissue level and organ level of biological organization.

rubric.why: Atoms join together to form molecules.
rubric.description: Describes the formation of molecules at the molecular level.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atoms combine to form molecules.

rubric.why: Small molecules can join to form larger biological molecules.
rubric.how: Award for stating that molecules form macromolecules or larger molecules.

rubric.why: Molecules are organized into cell structures, including organelles.
rubric.how: Award for relating molecules to the formation or structure of organelles.

rubric.why: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
rubric.description: Describes the cell level of organization.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the cell as the basic unit of life, or stating that organelles make up a cell.

modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules, and molecules can combine to form larger biological molecules.
These molecules form the structures of cell organelles.
At the cell level, organelles are organized within a cell and perform specific functions.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

items.followUp: Describe how food manufactured in leaves is transported through a plant.

rubric.why: Water enters the plant from the soil through root hairs by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award for identifying root hairs and osmosis as the route and process of water absorption.

rubric.why: Water passes through root tissues and enters the xylem.
rubric.description: Describes movement of water into root xylem.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water moves through the root to the xylem.

rubric.why: Xylem vessels conduct water from roots upwards through the stem.
rubric.how: Award for identifying xylem as the upward water-conducting tissue.

rubric.why: Water loss from leaves creates a pull that helps draw water upwards.
rubric.description: Explains the role of transpiration pull.
rubric.how: Award for linking transpiration to the upward movement of water.

rubric.why: A labeled diagram should show the continuous route of water through the plant.
rubric.description: Provides a clear, labeled transport diagram.
rubric.how: Award for a diagram or clear arrow sequence showing the route from roots through xylem to leaves; accept labels for root, stem, leaf, and/or stomata.

modelAnswer: Water in the soil enters root hairs by osmosis.
It moves through the root tissues and enters the xylem vessels.
Xylem transports water upwards through the roots and stem to the leaves.
Transpiration from the leaves creates a transpiration pull that helps draw water upwards.
Diagram: Soil water → root hair → root xylem → stem xylem ↑ → leaf xylem → leaf cells; water vapour exits through stomata.

items.followUp: Define a vulnerable species and give one example from Pakistan.

rubric.why: An endangered species faces a high risk of extinction.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the species is in danger of extinction; give both marks for a clear definition including the risk of disappearing.

rubric.why: Pakistan has several endangered animal species.
rubric.description: Names a suitable endangered species found in Pakistan.
rubric.how: Award for one valid Pakistan example, such as markhor, Indus river dolphin, snow leopard, or houbara bustard.

rubric.why: Human activities and habitat changes threaten these species.
rubric.description: States a reason species are endangered in Pakistan.
rubric.how: Award for one relevant threat, such as hunting, poaching, habitat loss, or pollution.

modelAnswer: An endangered species is a species whose numbers have fallen so much that it is at risk of extinction.
Examples of endangered species in Pakistan include the markhor, Indus river dolphin, snow leopard, and houbara bustard.
They are threatened by factors such as hunting and poaching, habitat loss, and pollution.

items.followUp: Explain how light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A limiting factor is one that restricts the rate of photosynthesis when in short supply.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the factor in shortest supply restricts the rate.

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award for relating light intensity to photosynthesis rate, including a plateau when another factor limits it.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so its concentration can limit the rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.how: Award for linking carbon dioxide availability with the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects its rate.
rubric.how: Award for stating that temperature affects the rate, preferably through enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Other necessary conditions, such as water and chlorophyll, may also limit photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award for naming water or chlorophyll as an additional factor that can limit photosynthesis.

modelAnswer: A limiting factor is a condition in short supply that restricts the rate of photosynthesis.
Light intensity affects the rate: as light intensity increases, the rate rises until another factor becomes limiting.
Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; a low concentration limits the rate, while increasing it raises the rate up to a limit.
Temperature affects the enzymes involved in photosynthesis; low temperatures slow the reactions and very high temperatures can damage enzymes.
Water and chlorophyll are also necessary, and a shortage of either can limit photosynthesis.

items.followUp: What is the function of chlorophyll in a plant cell?

rubric.why: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells.
rubric.how: Award for identifying plastids as organelles in plant cells, preferably noting their membrane-bound structure.

rubric.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award for naming chloroplasts and linking them to photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
rubric.how: Award for identifying chromoplasts as pigment-containing plastids that impart colour.

rubric.why: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids commonly involved in food storage.
rubric.how: Award for stating that leucoplasts are colourless and/or store food.

modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments and give colour to plant parts such as flowers and fruits.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food, such as starch, oils, or proteins.

items.followUp: Describe how the large intestine contributes to digestion and absorption.

rubric.why: Pancreatic juice enters the small intestine and provides enzymes for digestion.
rubric.description: Describes the role of pancreatic juice.
rubric.how: Award for stating that pancreatic enzymes act in the small intestine to digest food.

rubric.why: Bile helps make the conditions suitable for intestinal enzymes and emulsifies fats.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that bile neutralizes acidic chyme or emulsifies fats.

rubric.why: Intestinal enzymes complete the digestion of food molecules.
rubric.how: Award for stating that intestinal juice or its enzymes complete digestion.

rubric.why: Villi increase the surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.
rubric.how: Award for linking villi to absorption of digested food.

rubric.why: Digested nutrients pass into the blood, while many fats enter lacteals.
rubric.how: Award for stating that absorbed nutrients enter blood or that fats enter lacteals.

modelAnswer: In the small intestine, pancreatic juice supplies enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Bile from the liver neutralizes acidic food arriving from the stomach and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Enzymes in the intestinal juice complete the digestion of food into simple, soluble molecules.
The inner surface has many villi, which provide a large surface area for absorption.
Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood, while many products of fat digestion enter the lacteals.
